analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC fine drug companies that file baseless FDA petitions to delay generic competition.
analysis.headline: Backed by ten senators from both parties and reported out of the Judiciary Committee without dissent, the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes file petitions with the Food and Drug Administration claiming safety or manufacturing problems with a competing generic drug or biosimilar. If the petition is baseless, its real effect is to delay the competitor's approval, which keeps the brand-name company's monopoly prices in place longer. This bill would make filing an objectively baseless petition for that purpose an unfair method of competition, letting the Federal Trade Commission sue the filer and collect penalties of up to $50,000 for each day the FDA spent reviewing the petition.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who keep paying brand-name prices while generics are held up by delay petitions, and the generic and biosimilar makers whose products are being delayed. Faster approvals mean cheaper versions of drugs reach the market sooner.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair method of competition to submit an objectively baseless FDA petition aimed at interfering with a competitor's application for approval of a generic drug or biosimilar, and authorizes the FTC to sue the filer in federal court.

Sets the civil penalty at up to $50,000 for each calendar day the sham petition was under FDA review, or alternatively the revenue the filer earned on the drug during the review period — sized to erase the profit from the delay.

Creates a presumption that a petition is a sham if the Secretary of Health and Human Services determines its primary purpose was delaying approval and refers it to the FTC as part of a series of petitions, shifting the burden onto the filer to prove otherwise.

The bill's stated purpose also includes protecting the efficient review of petitions filed in good faith to raise legitimate public health concerns, so the penalty applies only to petitions that are objectively baseless.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers that use petitions to delay generic and biosimilar competitors, which would face FTC lawsuits and penalties, and would lose some of the extra months of monopoly-priced sales that delay tactics currently buy them.

drawbacks.text: Companies raising genuine safety or manufacturing concerns about a generic could now face FTC litigation risk, which could chill good-faith petitions even though the bill targets only objectively baseless ones and its own text commits to protecting legitimate public health petitions.

The potential penalty is large — a filer can be liable for the revenue earned on its drug during the entire review period — so even close-call petitions become expensive to defend, adding litigation costs to the regulatory process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: delaying a generic by even a few months can cost patients far more than the eventual penalty, so the bill changes the math on the delay tactic itself. The main honest objection is over-deterrence — a company with a legitimate safety worry might stay quiet rather than risk a lawsuit. But the bill requires the petition to be objectively baseless before any penalty applies, which is a fairly high bar, so the tradeoff favors patients and competition.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and placed it on the Senate's calendar of pending business in December 2021, but no one ever brought it to the floor for a vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on April 28, 2021 with nine original cosponsors spanning both parties, including Republicans Chuck Grassley, Joni Ernst, Ted Cruz, and Mike Braun.
The Senate referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which ordered it reported favorably without amendment in July 2021 and formally reported it on December 8, 2021.
The same day it was reported, it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 179), meaning it was cleared to come up for a floor vote at any time.
No further action ever occurred: the record shows no floor debate, no vote, and no House counterpart moving, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off: they keep the ability to file delay petitions with no risk of FTC penalties, and patients keep paying brand-name prices while cheaper generics wait in line. The bill had cleared every procedural hurdle short of a floor vote and died there anyway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers; patients kept paying more

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the bill's original cosponsors included 5 of 48 Senate Democrats and 4 of 50 Senate Republicans, and the Judiciary Committee reported it without amendment and without recorded opposition; the obstacle was the absence of floor time, not a partisan vote.

industries.note: Some brand-name companies file FDA petitions raising safety or manufacturing issues about competing generics; when baseless, the petition's real work is delaying approval, and every month of delay extends monopoly-priced sales. The bill attaches a penalty of up to $50,000 per day of review (or the drug's revenue during the delay period) to that tactic, directly cutting into the profit it generates.
Faster, cheaper FDA approval paths mean these companies can bring lower-priced versions of drugs to market sooner. Their gain — earlier competition — is the same thing patients gain.
